narrative:
The model estimated a 59.0% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because that is above the threshold used in this review, it treated bar failure as more likely than success, and your law school application was denied on that basis.

The strongest factor was your LSAT score. At 22.50, it is far below the 37.18 average for accepted students, and it pushed the prediction most strongly toward failure. The second strongest factor was your third-year class standing: you are in decile 1.00, while accepted students average around 5.79. That bottom-decile position also pushed strongly toward failure. Your high family income was the third most influential factor, but unlike the academic indicators it pushed toward passing rather than failure; it was simply not strong enough to offset the LSAT and third-year standing.

To move forward, ask admissions whether an appeal, reconsideration, or conditional admission path exists and what evidence they will accept. Consider retaking the LSAT with structured preparation, since a higher score would address the largest concern. Provide any context for your third-year ranking, such as extenuating circumstances, and ask whether updated grades or additional academic evidence could be reviewed. Meet with a pre-law advisor to build a concrete improvement plan before reapplying.
